ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: In each CQ and TQ wave, participants were assigned one of the five parallel blocks in the QEF.
Prior to Wave 1, we preregistered several exclusion criteria designed to filter out inattentive participants (see study preregistration).

During Wave 1, the first time participants completed multiple forecasting questions in a single sitting, median response times for the QEF questions ranged from 2.09 to 5.47 (IQR of medians = [2.76, 3.91]).
In each study, we recruited people to participate in a Rapid Fire Forecasting Challenge.
table.header: 4.4. The Future of Forecasting in Psychology

table.text: Participants were recruited between May 3, 2023 and May 15, 2023.
We recruited N = 100 participants via advertising on social media.
Participants had mean age of 40.67, SD = 14.07, 3,798 (61.5%) female, 2,170 (35.1%) male, 158 gender variant / non-conforming (2.6%), 8 something else (0.1%), 44 (0.8%) prefer not to say.
Participants were recruited between September 1, 2023 and September 15, 2023.
We recruited N = 1,199 participants via social media.
In the U-shaped condition, participants were paid $12.50 for completing the first wave, $5 for completing the second, and $12.50 for completing the third.
In the escalating condition, participants were paid $5 for completing the first wave, $10 for completing the second, and $15 for completing the third.
And in the backloaded condition, participants were paid $5 for completing each of the first two waves, and $20 for completing the third.
Participants who began with Wave 0 were recruited between September 1 st and 7 th of 2023, and completed two forecasting questions in each of the QEF and PEF.
Participants not in the Wave 0 condition were recruited between Procedure.
Participants are asked to assess the probability that several events occur within a series of increasing time horizons.
In this task, subjects are given a series of general knowledge problems with two possible answers.

> And in the backloaded condition, participants were paid $5 for completing each of the first two waves, and $20 for completing the third.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. -  We parsed 419 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
-  0 of 29 data columns (0%) are documented in a codebook; 29 are not.

For example, the codebook documents `G1472`, `C1084`, `G1190_t` while the data has `ID`, `Form`, `Question`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.

report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 3 codebook/README/label sources and 29 data columns across 3 files.

**A codebook was found and parsed (419 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents `G1472`, `C1084`, `G1190_t` while the data has `ID`, `Form`, `Question`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.**

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 29 columns across 3 data files.
#### Issues Identified

5 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: In each CQ and TQ wave, participants were assigned one of the five parallel blocks in the QEF.
Prior to Wave 1, we preregistered several exclusion criteria designed to filter out inattentive participants (see study preregistration).

During Wave 1, the first time participants completed multiple forecasting questions in a single sitting, median response times for the QEF questions ranged from 2.09 to 5.47 (IQR of medians = [2.76, 3.91]).
In each study, we recruited people to participate in a Rapid Fire Forecasting Challenge.
Participants were recruited between May 3, 2023 and May 15, 2023.
We recruited N = 100 participants via advertising on social media.
Participants had mean age of 40.67, SD = 14.07, 3,798 (61.5%) female, 2,170 (35.1%) male, 158 gender variant / non-conforming (2.6%), 8 something else (0.1%), 44 (0.8%) prefer not to say.
Participants were recruited between September 1, 2023 and September 15, 2023.
We recruited N = 1,199 participants via social media.
In the U-shaped condition, participants were paid $12.50 for completing the first wave, $5 for completing the second, and $12.50 for completing the third.
In the escalating condition, participants were paid $5 for completing the first wave, $10 for completing the second, and $15 for completing the third.
And in the backloaded condition, participants were paid $5 for completing each of the first two waves, and $20 for completing the third.
Participants who began with Wave 0 were recruited between September 1 st and 7 th of 2023, and completed two forecasting questions in each of the QEF and PEF.
Participants not in the Wave 0 condition were recruited between Procedure.
Participants are asked to assess the probability that several events occur within a series of increasing time horizons.
In this task, subjects are given a series of general knowledge problems with two possible answers.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 3 R code files.
#### Run order

A dependency **cycle** was detected among 2 files (Enhancing reliability in the identification of forecaster talent.R, Psychometric properties of probability and quantile forecasts.R): each reads a file another writes, so no run order satisfies all of them. This must be resolved before the code can run.

```{r}

    "Runs after" = "—", Basis = "none"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 4 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `scores_quantile.csv`, `scores_probability with pre-set bins.csv`, `summary_scores_all_tasks_by_subject_id.csv`, `itnames.csv`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 3 scripts: 0 ran without error, 1 errored, 2 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

text.text: Accurate predictions about the future are crucial for optimizing policy choices, but finding skilled forecasters is challenging.

Prior work relied on forecasting tournaments to identify generalist "superforecasters" who made accurate predictions across domains, but these tournaments take months to complete and require large concurrent samples to compare performance among individuals.
We solve these problems by developing a one-hour Forecasting Proficiency Test (FPT) that explains 75% of the variance in forecasters' accuracy about a wide variety of events.

The FPT provides standardized percentile scores normed to a large (N = 1, 147) test development sample based on a combination of reusable real-world forecasting questions and standalone cognitive tests.
Which questions and tests are included is highly customizable.

Forecasting questions are the best predictors of forecasting proficiency, but cognitive tests help stabilize score distributions and facilitate score exchangeability across different custom test versions even as forecasting questions and resolution dates change.
The FPT is primarily a practical tool for decision-makers who rely on accurate predictions to make decisions.

However, it is based on one of the largest dedicated psychometric studies ever conducted on human forecasting, which also provides insight into the cognitive mechanisms that drive forecasting proficiency and guidance for future researchers interested in studying the psychology of forecasting.
In 2010, the U.S. intelligence community launched the largest human-subjects forecasting study ever conducted: the Aggregative Contingent Estimation study, better known as ACE.
Several research teams were funded to compete against one another in an effort to put together the most accurate judgmental forecasting system possible.

The winning research team, the Good Judgment Project, made a crucial discovery that aided their success: it was possible to identify remarkably skilled generalist forecasters, or superforecasters, who reliably made accurate predictions spanning a wide range of domains (Mellers et al. 2014 , 2015a ,b, Tetlock and Gardner 2015).
text.formatted: The winning research team, the Good Judgment Project, made a crucial discovery that aided their success: it was possible to identify remarkably skilled generalist forecasters, or superforecasters, who reliably made accurate predictions spanning a wide range of domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Mellers et al. 2014</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2015a</ref> <ref type="bibr">,b, Tetlock and Gardner 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Since ACE, scientific interest in the nature of forecasting proficiency and its role in optimizing forecasting systems has grown substantially.

This includes research on psychological predictors of forecasting performance (Atanasov and Himmelstein 2023 , Himmelstein et al. 2021 , Mellers et al. 2015a , Merkle et al. 2026), psychometric models of forecasting proficiency (Bo et al. 2017 , Himmelstein et al. 2021 , Merkle et al. 2016 , Setti et al. 2026), how forecasting proficiency measurement can help aggregate forecasts (Budescu and Chen 2015 , Collins et al. 2023 , Davis-Stober et al. 2014 , Han and Budescu 2019), training forecasters (Chang et al. 2016), forecasting teams (Mellers et al. 2014), and peer comparisons (Helmer et al. 2026 , Himmelstein et al. 2023 , Witkowski et al. 2017).
text.formatted: This includes research on psychological predictors of forecasting performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Atanasov and Himmelstein 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">, Himmelstein et al. 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr">, Mellers et al. 2015a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">, Merkle et al. 2026)</ref>, psychometric models of forecasting proficiency <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bo et al. 2017</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">, Himmelstein et al. 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">, Merkle et al. 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">, Setti et al. 2026)</ref>, how forecasting proficiency measurement can help aggregate forecasts <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Budescu and Chen 2015</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">, Collins et al. 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">, Davis-Stober et al. 2014</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">, Han and Budescu 2019)</ref>, training forecasters <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Chang et al. 2016)</ref>, forecasting teams <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Mellers et al. 2014)</ref>, and peer comparisons <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Helmer et al. 2026</ref> <ref type="bibr">, Himmelstein et al. 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">, Witkowski et al. 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Despite this explosion of interest, existing tools for measuring forecasting proficiency are inefficient, and it remains unclear if forecasting proficiency is even a well defined psychological construct.
The majority of relevant research still comes from the original ACE datasets, as well as a follow-up study: the Hybrid Forecasting Competition (HFC; Benjamin et al. 2023).
text.formatted: The majority of relevant research still comes from the original ACE datasets, as well as a follow-up study: the Hybrid Forecasting Competition (HFC; <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Benjamin et al. 2023</ref>).

text.text: These were not dedicated psychological studies, but lengthy forecasting tournaments meant to generate insights across a wide range of disciplines.
Superforecaster identification required eliciting forecasts about hundreds of questions over the course of several months or years-a massive time, effort, and resource investment.
Developing efficient psychometric instruments for human forecasting proficiency requires a more specialized research design (Himmelstein et al. 2023 , Hauenstein et al. 2025).
text.formatted: Developing efficient psychometric instruments for human forecasting proficiency requires a more specialized research design <ref type="bibr">(Himmelstein et al. 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">, Hauenstein et al. 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The purpose of this project was to determine if forecasting proficiency can be measured with a Forecasting Proficiency Test (FPT).
text.formatted: The purpose of this project was to determine if forecasting proficiency can be measured with a Forecasting Proficiency Test <ref type="bibr">(FPT)</ref>.

text.text: This is primarily an empirical question: how well can a standalone instrument predict future forecasting performance?
Benchmarks from forecasting tournament research indicate that with sufficient data approximately 50-60% of the variance in such individual differences is explainable (Himmelstein et al. 2021).
text.formatted: Benchmarks from forecasting tournament research indicate that with sufficient data approximately 50-60% of the variance in such individual differences is explainable <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Himmelstein et al. 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Our dedicated FPT exceeds those benchmarks, explaining approximately 75% of the variance in forecasting performance on an outof-sample question set while requiring only a fraction of the resource investment.
To achieve this, the FPT relies on two distinct types of instruments: real-world forecasting questions and standalone cognitive tests.
From a purely predictive perspective, our results suggest the forecasting questions alone may be sufficient for measuring forecasting proficiency.
However, inclusion of separate cognitive tests provides a hedge against some of the limitations of relying solely on forecasting questions while maintaining comparable predictive performance.
Cognitive tests can also offer information about the particular strengths and weaknesses of a given forecaster that forecasting questions cannot.
While we recommend using a mixture of both components, the specific form of the test is highly customizable.
There are two key pillars in psychometric instrument development: reliability and validity.
Reliability refers to the how consistent an instrument is.

Different aspects of reliability include internal consistency (how correlated scores from different test items are with one another) and test-retest reliability (how stable measurements are about the same people over time).
Validity refers to the fidelity with which an instrument measures what it is intended to.

Aspects of validity include construct validity (whether measurements adequately represent an underlying psychological theory) and criterion validity (whether they are adequately predictive of future performance).
An FPT has an atypical psychometric development profile.
On the one hand, criterion validity is unusually easy to evaluate.

In more traditional settings, criterion validity refers to predictions about future academic or job performance, which often have a long time horizon between test administration and criterion resolution, making them challenging to evaluate during the test development process.
An FPT has a very clear criterion: predicting how accurate a forecaster tends to be on real-world forecasting questions.

There is a robust literature on how to quantify forecasting accuracy (Gneiting and Raftery 2007, Merkle and Steyvers 2013), so criterion validity for an FPT is easily operationalized by examining how well test scores predict accuracy on an out-of-sample set of forecasting questions.
text.formatted: There is a robust literature on how to quantify forecasting accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Gneiting and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Raftery 2007, Merkle and</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Steyvers 2013)</ref>, so criterion validity for an FPT is easily operationalized by examining how well test scores predict accuracy on an out-of-sample set of forecasting questions.

text.text: However, on the other hand, the scoring rules typically used in forecasting tournaments have poor reliability (Himmelstein et al. 2023).
text.formatted: However, on the other hand, the scoring rules typically used in forecasting tournaments have poor reliability <ref type="bibr">(Himmelstein et al. 2023)</ref>.

text.text: One consequence of poor reliability is a commensurate increase in measurement error.

The most brute force way to improve reliability is to increase the total number of items on a test, which is why in forecasting tournaments so many questions are needed before superforecasters can be reliably identified.

Thus, if forecasting questions are either to be used for criterion validity or as test items themselves, it is crucial to improve reliability without requiring an impractically large number of questions.
Elicitation Format One of the most consequential decisions for determining the psychometric reliability of forecast accuracy metrics is how those forecasts are elicited (Zhu et al. 2026).
text.formatted: Elicitation Format One of the most consequential decisions for determining the psychometric reliability of forecast accuracy metrics is how those forecasts are elicited <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Zhu et al. 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Studies like ACE and HFC relied on the probability elicitation format (PEF), also referred to as the fixed-variable format, for elicitation.

This approach discretizes the outcome distribution into a set of mutually exclusive and exhaustive options and asks forecasters to assign probabilities to each bin (Benjamin et al. 2023 , Himmelstein and Budescu 2023 , Mellers et al. 2014).
text.formatted: This approach discretizes the outcome distribution into a set of mutually exclusive and exhaustive options and asks forecasters to assign probabilities to each bin <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Benjamin et al. 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr">, Himmelstein and Budescu 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">, Mellers et al. 2014)</ref>.

text.text: For an example of a PEF question, see Figure 1a.
text.formatted: For an example of a PEF question, see Figure <ref type="figure">1a</ref>.

text.text: Accuracy scores from questions in the PEF suffer from poor internal consistency due to the fact that they are scored based on discrete, rather than continuous resolution criteria (Aldous 2021 , Himmelstein et al. 2023 , Zhu et al. 2026).
text.formatted: Accuracy scores from questions in the PEF suffer from poor internal consistency due to the fact that they are scored based on discrete, rather than continuous resolution criteria <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Aldous 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr">, Himmelstein et al. 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr">, Zhu et al. 2026</ref>).

text.text: An alternative option is the quantile elicitation format (QEF), also known as the fixed-probability format. 1 The QEF requires forecasters to report quantiles associated with fixed probabilities of a continuous variable's cumulative density function (Abbas et al. 2008 , Jose and Winkler 2009 , Palley and Bansal 2021).
text.formatted: An alternative option is the quantile elicitation format (QEF), also known as the fixed-probability format. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">1</ref> The QEF requires forecasters to report quantiles associated with fixed probabilities of a continuous variable's cumulative density function <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abbas et al. 2008</ref> <ref type="bibr">, Jose and Winkler 2009</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">, Palley and Bansal 2021)</ref>.

text.text: See Figure 1b for an example of a QEF forecasting question.
text.formatted: See Figure <ref type="figure">1b</ref> for an example of a QEF forecasting question.

text.text: Based on the dataset reported in this paper as well as a separate dataset from a recent forecasting study (Karger et al. 2021), Zhu et al. (2026) found QEF scores reach suitable levels of reliability in fewer questions than the PEF because they are based on continuous rather than discrete resolution criteria.
text.formatted: Based on the dataset reported in this paper as well as a separate dataset from a recent forecasting study <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Karger et al. 2021)</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Zhu et al. (2026)</ref> found QEF scores reach suitable levels of reliability in fewer questions than the PEF because they are based on continuous rather than discrete resolution criteria.

text.text: Question Reusability One complication inherent in using real-world forecasting questions on a test is that they are temporally specific: they have fixed resolution dates on which the ground truth is determined.
Some forecasting questions can be repeated for different resolution dates, such as "What will the price of gold be on [date]?"
text.formatted: Some forecasting questions can be repeated for different resolution dates, such as "What will the price of gold be on <ref type="bibr">[date]</ref>?"

text.text: These typically involve continuous time series variables.

Because the question stem can be reused by changing the resolution date, these types of questions are potentially suitable for the FPT, even though the resolution will be different any time the date is changed.

The QEF has an additional advantage for such questions over the PEF: the fixed probability values never need change either within or between questions, while in the PEF, the bins must be set based on the item-writer's judgment and kept up to date as the question is reused over time.

Other forecasting questions can only be asked about a specific date, and then never again, such as "What will the Supreme Court Decide in Salazar V. Paramount Global?", an upcoming case which remains undecided at the time of this writing.
These are often categorical events rather than continuous time series, and thus must be elicited in the PEF.
Their poor reliability and lack of reusability make them unsuitable for FPT inclusion.
While the QEF solves the reliability problem, it introduces a new one: accuracy scores for QEF questions are defined by the scale of the variable being forecasted (Jose and Winkler 2009).
text.formatted: While the QEF solves the reliability problem, it introduces a new one: accuracy scores for QEF questions are defined by the scale of the variable being forecasted <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Jose and Winkler 2009)</ref>.

text.text: If different questions are about variables that have very different scales, accuracy scores must somehow be standardized so they can be combined into a composite score.

A natural approach would be to standardize accuracy scores relative to a large sample of forecasters, so for each item, scores have a mean of zero, and deviations are in Z-score units relative to the sample mean.

This approach, which we refer to as sample standardization, is commonly used for PEF questions in forecasting tournaments to account for differences in question difficulty (Atanasov and Himmelstein 2023).
text.formatted: This approach, which we refer to as sample standardization, is commonly used for PEF questions in forecasting tournaments to account for differences in question difficulty <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Atanasov and Himmelstein 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, even for questions with reusable stems, this approach would require constantly re-norming questions each time the resolution date changes, making it impractical for the FPT.
We solve this problem with an approach we refer to as historical standardization.
Prior to scoring, we standardize each forecast and resolution relative to the mean and standard deviation of the question's historical time series.
This transforms forecasts and resolutions into Z-score deviations from the historical average, putting all forecasts, and thus accuracy scores, on similar scales.
Criterion validity alone is not sufficient to make the FPT practically useful.

Historical standardization facilitates aggregation of accuracy scores across variables on very different scales, but by itself does not account for variations in question difficulty or produce scores that can be interpreted in the context of population norms.

Forecasting questions are the cornerstone of the FPT that supports criterion validity, but an outstanding question is if they can produce scores that are stable and which can be interpreted relative to population norms.

This is where the primary value of the cognitive tests comes into play: while on their own they have lower criterion validity, using cognitive tests to complement forecasting questions can help stabilize score distributions relative to population norms.
During test development, we compared several versions of the FPT which varied in terms of how heavily they relied on forecasting questions or cognitive tests.
In addition to testing their criterion validity, we also tested the sensitivity of FPT percentile scores to their own reference distribution.

The FPT version that relied entirely on forecasting questions had average errors of 7.5 percentile points when transforming raw scores to percentiles based on distributions normed on separate subsamples of forecasters and forecasting questions.

However, when the test replaced 20-40% of the forecasting questions with cognitive tests, this average error dropped to 5.4-6.0 percentile points while maintaining comparable criterion validity to the fully forecasting-questionbased FPT.
These results show that adding cognitive tests reduced percentile discrepancies for scores based on different question sets.
They also provide indirect evidence that supplementing diverse forecasting questions with cognitive components may reduce sensitivity to temporal shifts in score distributions.
Future research should test this possibility directly by administering the same question stems with different resolution dates.
In ACE and HFC, participants began with an intake survey that included a number of objective cognitive tests and subjective personality assessments (Himmelstein et al. 2021 , Mellers et al. 2015a).

text.text: Most importantly for our purposes, they can complement real-world forecasting problems whose score distributions change over time by providing scores from more stable distributions.
Because the FPT is meant to be an incentive compatible test of ability we chose to exclude subjective self-report scales during test development and instead rely solely on objective cognitive tests.
In this section, we briefly review the types of cognitive tests used in ACE and HFC as well as new cognitive test candidates we implemented for potential FPT inclusion.
We also discuss how these tests help refine the notion of forecasting proficiency as a psychological construct and contribute to our understanding of its relationship to general human intelligence.
In ACE And HFC, cognitive tests primarily focused on numerical reasoning and fluid intelligence.
Examples appearing in each study included variations on the Berlin Numeracy Test (Cokely et al. 2012), the Cognitive Reflection Test (Frederick 2005), and Raven's Progressive Matrices (Raven 2000).

text.text: In a perfect world, the FPT would be made up entirely of cognitive tests that could be reused indefinitely without requiring changes to question resolutions.
While we neither expected to nor achieved that goal, we did want to see if we could improve diagnosticity by bringing new cognitive tests into the mix.

This included a combination of psychometrically validated tests that were strong theoretical candidates to be predictive of forecasting performance, but which had not been used in ACE or HFC, such as the Adult Decision Making Competence Inventory (Bruine de Bruin et al. 2007), the Graph Literacy Test (Galesic and Garcia-Retamero 2011), and the Coherence Forecasting Scale (Ho et al. 2024).

text.text: It also included several new tests that had not been previously validated as psychometric instruments.

These were inspired by prior research on topics such as metacognitive judgment (Bennett and Steyvers 2022), base rate sensitivity (Garcia-Retamero et al. 2010), information search (Knox et al. 2012), adherence to Bayes' rule (Phillips and Edwards 1966), and time series extrapolation (Reimers and Harvey 2011).

text.text: While the primary goal of this project is empirical-producing an instrument capable of predicting forecasters' future performance (criterion validity)-it also contributes to an important theoretical question: is forecasting proficiency a valid psychological construct?
This question cuts in two directions: (1) Is forecasting proficiency distinct from existing notions of general intelligence?
(2) Is forecasting proficiency a singular psychological construct, or a multi-dimensional combination of distinct facets?
While our study design limits potential contributions to the latter question, it does provide some evidence about the former.

General human intelligence, often referred to as the g-factor, is defined by the positive manifold: the finding that the correlations among variables related to human intelligence are consistently large and positive.
Correlations between forecasting performance and existing measures of intelligence empirically confirm forecasting proficiency fits into the positive manifold (Atanasov and Himmelstein 2023).
text.formatted: Correlations between forecasting performance and existing measures of intelligence empirically confirm forecasting proficiency fits into the positive manifold <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Atanasov and Himmelstein 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Determining whether forecasting taps into cognitive faculties not captured by these existing measures means testing if other, theoretically motivated measures better predict forecasting performance.
We found that several of our newly developed cognitive tests predict forecasting performance better than other previously existing measures.

Though a study more explicitly oriented towards construct validity would help to validate this result, and it says little about the dimensionality structure of forecasting proficiency as a psychological construct, it represents preliminary evidence that forecasting proficiency may be distinct aspect of human intelligence.

text.text: The primary study took place over approximately 10 weeks between March and May of 2024.
The first three weeks focused on recruitment (see details below), while the study itself occurred across seven weekly waves.

Because we were using accuracy on different sets of real-world forecasting questions as both the criterion and a test component candidate, we preregistered different subsets of questions to serve in each role for each participant.
This approach ensured we did not opportunistically take advantage of correlational results by using the same forecasting questions as predictors for some analyses and criteria in other analyses.
Criterion forecasting questions (CQs) refer to those questions for which accuracy scores serve as response variables in subsequent analyses.
Test candidate questions (TQs) refer to those for which accuracy scores serve as predictor variables.
Waves 1 and 7 consisted entirely of CQs in both the QEF and PEF.
Waves 2, 4, and 6 consisted entirely of TQs.

Because PEF questions are less reliable and require item writers to select and maintain bins over time, and setting sensible bins can inadvertently leak information about the expected outcome distribution to testees, TQs focused exclusively on the QEF.
Waves 3 and 5 consisted of cognitive tests.
Based on results of pilot studies 1 and 2 (see Appendix A.1), we selected 36 forecasting questions to use in the primary study.
All questions were continuous time series and thus could be posed in both the QEF and PEF and repeated with different resolution dates.

These questions had been sorted into six categories: Economics, Marketing, and Finance; Energy and Technology; Environment and Agriculture; Politics, Demography, Immigration, and Crime; Health and Medicine; and Entertainment and Media.
They were grouped into six blocks of six questions such that no block had more than two questions from any category.
This ensured that no block was too heavily weighted towards a particular domain of expertise.
Five of these blocks (Blocks A through E) were classified as parallel blocks.
In each CQ and TQ wave, participants were assigned one of the five parallel blocks in the QEF.
There were five unique sequences of parallel blocks by wave, which we refer to as order conditions.
These were chosen by a Latin square design (see Table 1).

Automatic Item Generation.
For several of the cognitive tests, it is possible to randomize elements of their content or procedurally generate a very large bank from which individual test items can be drawn.
In the psychometric literature this is known as Automatic Item Generation (AIG; Gierl and Haladyna 2013).
AIG ensures that testees are unable to memorize test items before taking the test.
However, when developing an AIG-based test, it is important to establish that the different randomized versions of the tests produce exchangeable scores.
This can be validated during test development by including a fixed set of items, referred to as an anchor version.
Demonstrating that scores from anchor and AIG-based versions of a test produce comparable scores is a method of validating exchangeability.
AIG results are discussed in Appendix C. Cognitive Test Sequencing.
Cognitive tests were split into two blocks with comparable expected durations based on the results of pilot study 3.
Waves 3 and 5 each included one cognitive test block.
For tests with AIG versions, the AIG and anchor versions were assigned to different blocks, so both versions never appeared within the same wave.
The wave in which each block was administered was randomized for each participant between waves 3 and 5.

Recruitment, Exclusion Criteria, and Incentives 2.2.1.
General Population Recruitment took place in early March of 2024.
An existing panel of participants from the Quorum research platform was invited to participate.
We also ran recruitment advertisements on Facebook and Instagram during this period.

All participants who responded to an invitation or advertisement began with an introductory wave (Wave 0), which consisted of one PEF forecasting question, one QEF forecasting question, Berlin Numeracy (Cokely et al. 2012), and two attention checks (see Appendix E).
All participants who completed Wave 0 and passed both attention checks were invited to participate in Wave 1.
Prior to Wave 1, we preregistered several exclusion criteria designed to filter out inattentive participants (see study preregistration).
All participants who were not excluded following Wave 1 were invited to Wave 2.
For remaining waves, the only exclusion criterion was failure to complete the prior wave, and completion of each wave guaranteed an invitation to the subsequent wave.
Beginning with Wave 1, participants received escalating payments for participation.
They were paid $5 for Waves 1-3, $10 for Waves 4-5, $15 for Wave 6, and $25 for Wave 7.
Each wave also included performance incentives.
During Wave 0, the top 50 performers received a $10 bonus.
During each subsequent wave, the top 25 performers received a $25 bonus.
Performance was calculated as a sum of standardized scores across all forecasting questions and cognitive tests within a wave.
We also invited a number of previously established superforecasters to participate.

Superforecasters were defined as participants who either finished in the top 2% in accuracy in the original ACE study (Mellers et al. 2015b) or were classified as such by Good Judgment Inc. 6 based on their accuracy on a set of similar forecasting questions.

Results have indicated that a) the QEF produces accuracy scores with superior reliability to the PEF, b) historical standardization facilitates combining questions on different scales into a composite score without requiring a large sample to standardize individual question scores, and c) TQ accuracy is the best predictor of CQ accuracy, but cognitive tests can provide complementary predictive information.
Based on these results, we propose five different versions of the FPT which vary in how heavily they rely on TQs versus cognitive tests.
For consistency, we chose to make each version approximately one hour in length, a somewhat arbitrary choice designed to balance collecting sufficient information with a manageable test length.
To maintain this approximate length across test versions, we examined the response times of the forecasting questions and cognitive tests.

During Wave 1, the first time participants completed multiple forecasting questions in a single sitting, median response times for the QEF questions ranged from 2.09 to 5.47 (IQR of medians = [2.76, 3.91]).

text.text: Four of the order conditions were used as a training sample to estimate the model in eq. 8, with one testing order condition held out for validation.
For example, when order condition 1 was held out, the model was trained on data from order conditions 2-5, and predictions were made on data from order condition 1.

This partitioning is natural because it means that in each fold, the model is trained and tested on a separate set of forecasters and forecasting questions-neither the forecasters or CQs the models are trained on appear in their testing samples.
Because we wished to keep proposed FPT versions to approximately one hour in length, none of them could include all of the TQs, so we bootstrapped the procedure.

A final outstanding question is how well test components discriminate forecasters in different ranges of the skill distribution.
We used three thresholds of M SA n from the CQ waves to define the ranges of interest: the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles.

We used two approaches to test how well predictor variables discriminated whether forecasters were above or below each threshold: a standardized mean differences (Cohen's d) approach and a signal detection theory approach.
We calculated Cohen's d for test components comparing groups of forecasters who were above and below each specified threshold.
This method is useful for determining which specific predictors might be especially informative about high or low proficiency forecasters.
Figure 7 shows absolute Cohen's d values comparing forecasters above and below the specified M SA n thresholds from the CQ waves for the predictors used in the dominance analysis in Table 4.

For the signal detection analysis, we fit binary logistic regression models that predicted whether forecasters were above or below each threshold and produced ROC curves.

An ROC curve shows the sensitivity, or the proportion of correct positive classifications out of total positive cases, and specificity, or the proportion of correct negative classifications out of total negative cases.
Sensitivity and specificity trade off depending on whether one is willing to tolerate more false positives or false negatives.

For example, if we are trying to predict the probability that a forecaster is above the 90th percentile of M SA n from the CQ waves, and we want to be very careful to limit the number of forecasters below the 90th percentile that we incorrectly include, we could insist on clearing a high bar for specificity.
The corresponding sensitivity would then tell us how many forecasters above the 90th percentile we correctly included and how many we missed by setting such a conservative threshold.

If, on the other hand, we wanted to limit the number of forecasters above the 90th percentile that we miss out on, even if it means incorrectly including some forecasters below the 90th percentile, we could insist on a high sensitivity.
The corresponding specificity would tell us how many forecasters below the 90th percentile we incorrectly included.
The area under the curve (AUC) is a global measure of how well a classification model performs across all levels of sensitivity and specificity.
Perfect classifications would yield an AUC of 1.0, while random guessing would have an expected AUC of 0.5.
Logistic regressions used predictors from FPT Version 3 using the same cross-validation logic as prior analyses.
For each fold, 16 we fit three logistic regression models in the training samples: one for each of the specified thresholds.
Each model was then used to predict the probability participants in the testing sample were above or below the specified thresholds.

How much can we learn about the proficiency of a forecaster in just one hour?
As it turns out, quite a lot.
The FPT is capable of explaining approximately 75% of the variance in individual forecasters' performance across a variety of real-world forecasting questions from different domains.
Prior to the FPT, the gold standard for identifying talented forecasters was to hold months-long forecasting tournaments among hundreds of forecasters.

The FPT can not only be administered to a single forecaster in just one hour, but also can explain even more about their forecasting proficiency than running them through a typical forecasting tournament would.
The FPT is not just informative, but also customizable.
It can contain combinations of both reusable real-world forecasting questions and standalone cognitive tests.

The versions of the FPT with the strongest criterion validity, as measured by its ability to predict individual differences in accuracy on out-of-sample forecasting questions, relied primarily on these questions.
However, scores based on different blocks of questions were only moderately exchangeable.

Transforming raw FPT scores to percentiles based distributions normed on different question blocks led to errors, on average, of approximately eight percentile points in how individuals compared to the rest of the test development sample.

Combining slightly fewer real-world forecasting questions with a handful of more stable cognitive tests reduced these errors to approximately five percentile points with minimal loss in criterion validity.

Cognitive tests also address the cold start problem: the cognitive tests can be scored immediately, providing a preliminary, albeit weaker measure of forecasting proficiency right away without having to wait for forecasting questions to resolve.
Superiority of QEF One of the key results from this project, explored in greater depth by Zhu et al. (2026), is how much more reliable accuracy scores from the QEF are than the scores from the PEF.
text.formatted: Superiority of QEF One of the key results from this project, explored in greater depth by <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Zhu et al. (2026)</ref>, is how much more reliable accuracy scores from the QEF are than the scores from the PEF.

text.text: However, unlike scoring rules for the PEF, such as the Brier and logarithmic scoring rules, S-scores, the proper scores used to evaluate QEFs, are sensitive to the scale of the variable being forecasted.
This makes them challenging to combine into a composite person-level score.
We solve this challenge with a method we refer to as historical standardization.
Historical standardization standardizes both the forecasts and question resolutions prior to scoring for accuracy based on each question's historical time series.
The resultant S-scores are scale-free, and can thus be combined into composite person-level composites.
It is important to note that the benefits we find in the QEF are psychometric: QEFs are better for measuring forecasting proficiency, but that does not imply they produce more accurate forecasts.
More research is needed to compare how the accuracy of forecasts might vary as a function of elicitation format.
The conclusions presented in this paper are focused on person-level forecasting proficiency measurement.
The FPT is intended to be a publicly available resource, but this poses a potential problem: item exposure.
If testees become too familiar with the specific questions on some of the cognitive tests, that would invalidate those tests as measurement instruments.

Fortunately, our results demonstrate that two of the most informative cognitive tests, denominator neglect and Bayesian updating, are conducive to Automatic Item Generation, which means their content can change dynamically each time they are administered.
This was a significant factor in prioritizing their inclusion in the FPT.
The FPT can reliably identify the best forecasters in the population.
However, it is even more successful at identifying the worst forecasters, which suggests there may be room for improvement in elite talent identification.
All of the results in this paper rely on parametric linear modeling frameworks.

Given the high degree of total variance we are able to explain in forecasters' accuracy, it is unlikely more complex nonlinear or nonparametric models would provide substantial gains across the full population distribution, but there is potential to increase the signal-to-noise ratio specifically in the upper range of the distribution.
Follow-up research may wish to consider the extent to which predictive performance can be improved for elite forecasting talent.
The FPT was an ambitious and expensive project.
To optimize cost effectiveness, we chose to limit data collection to instruments that could serve as potential test components as much as possible.

Because of this, our results speak most directly to forecasting proficiency for the types of forecasting problems that can be administered on a test: continuous time series questions with time horizons on the order of weeks to months, rather than years.
Future research should seek to generalize the usefulness of the FPT to other types of forecasting problems and longer time horizons.
The purpose of the FPT project was primarily empirical, which is why we prioritized criterion validity over construct validity.
However, our results do provide some insight about the notion of forecasting proficiency as a psychological construct, and point towards important new research directions worth pursuing.

Several newly developed cognitive tests, such as denominator neglect and Bayesian updating, as well as previously validated tests, such as the cognitive reflection test (Frederick 2005) and the adherence to decision rules subscale of the Adult Decision-Making Competence Inventory (Bruine de Bruin et al. 2007), predicted forecasting proficiency better than common measures of general intelligence and numerical reasoning ability.
text.formatted: Several newly developed cognitive tests, such as denominator neglect and Bayesian updating, as well as previously validated tests, such as the cognitive reflection test <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Frederick 2005)</ref> and the adherence to decision rules subscale of the Adult Decision-Making Competence Inventory (Bruine de <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bruin et al. 2007</ref>), predicted forecasting proficiency better than common measures of general intelligence and numerical reasoning ability.

text.text: This is evidence that these tests tap into skills that distinctly drive forecasting proficiency, and provides a direction for future research more focused on theoretical construct validity.
Additionally, our results say little about the dimensionality structure of forecasting proficiency.
Like the big forecasting tournaments, we intentionally operationalized forecasting proficiency by using a diverse set of questions that come from a variety of domains.
The purpose of this choice was to maximally separate forecasting skill from domain expertise.
However, forecasting proficiency may well be inseparable from domain expertise.
Future research should focus on clearly operationalizing forecasting domains of interest, rather than remaining agnostic to their idiosyncrasies.
Human forecasting ability is a topic that has generated substantial interest in recent years (Tetlock and Gardner 2015, Atanasov and Himmelstein 2023).

text.text: However, most recent advances in the field came from studies that were not truly designed to study the psychology of forecasting, but rather the role of crowd wisdom in broader forecasting systems (Benjamin et al. 2023 , Mellers et al. 2015b).
text.formatted: However, most recent advances in the field came from studies that were not truly designed to study the psychology of forecasting, but rather the role of crowd wisdom in broader forecasting systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Benjamin et al. 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr">, Mellers et al. 2015b)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond creating a new gold standard instrument for measuring forecasting proficiency, the FPT project also shows what is possible with dedicated psychological research on human forecasting.
We hope that our results not only help humanity make better forecasts, but inspire more psychologists to continue to study how better forecasts can be made.
The questions must be timeless, where timelessness is defined as being reusable for an arbitrary resolution date.
For example, "What will the price of gold be on December 1, 2022" is a timeless question, because the date can be changed to any other future date and remain a sensible question.
A non-timeless question would be "Who will the United States Supreme Court rule in favor of in the case of Students for Fair Admissions v.
Harvard?"
because once this question resolves, it cannot equivalently be asked again for a different future time horizon.

The questions must be resolvable, where resolvability refers to the existence of one or more databases that can be used to determine the outcomes of questions, and that can be reported to participants so they clearly understand how the outcome of the question will be determined.
We also checked how regularly resolvability databases were updated.
Any database that was updated inconsistently or irregularly was omitted.
Questions that could be asked about multiple different geographic locations were prioritized.
For example, "What will the pm2.5 air quality rating be for Beijing, China on August 1, 2023 be?"
Can be asked equivalently about regions other than Beijing.
Questions that featured highly duplicative content were de-duplicated.
This procedure ultimately left us with a set of 140 questions under consideration for Pilot Study 1A and 1B.
A list of these questions can be found at https://osf.io/q2e94/.
text.formatted: A list of these questions can be found at <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/q2e94/">https://osf.io/q2e94/</ref>.

text.text: We next wanted to filter these 140 questions down 36 questions to be used in the primary study.
We wanted a set of questions that was diverse content wise, and did not clearly favor any particular domain expertise.
To accomplish this, we sought to collect a sufficiently large amount of pairwise observations between all possible pairs of questions and analyze correlational patterns between the questions.
In each study, we recruited people to participate in a Rapid Fire Forecasting Challenge.
People were randomly given a sequence of forecasting problems and could answer as many or as few as they wished.
Because we didn't want people to invest substantial time, forecasting problems were timed.
If participants did not respond before the timer expired, they were moved to the next question.
They were not given any baseline compensation for participation, but for each question they answered, they were entered into a lottery for which they could win a monetary prize.
They were also awarded additional entries for making accurate forecasts.
Pilot Study 1A was a testing and planning study for Pilot Study 1B.

Besides testing the study program and recruitment approach, we also wanted to get a ballpark estimate of how feasible it would be to collect a large number of pairwise observations for all pairs of the 140 questions.
Participants.
Participants were recruited between May 3, 2023 and May 15, 2023.
We recruited N = 100 participants via advertising on social media.
We did not collect demographic information during the pilot.
Procedure.
We randomly selected 50 of the 140 questions we planned to use in Pilot Study 1B.
Participants who registered were randomly assigned a sequence of questions.

For each question, they had three minutes to provide a single best estimate for the outcome (all questions were about continuous numerical outcomes), as well as provide a rating using a continuous slider that ranged from 1 to 100 in terms of their familiarity with the question; their confidence in their prediction; how much the forecast depended on the particular time of week, month, or year (seasonality); and how much the difficulty in making a prediction about that question is a result of their lack of personal knowledge rather than lack of predictability ("aleatoryness").
If they did not submit a response within three minutes, they were moved to the next question.
All questions had resolution dates at the end of May 2023.
For an example of an question, see Figure A1.
text.formatted: For an example of an question, see Figure <ref type="figure">A1</ref>.

text.text: For each question, any participant who submitted a response to that question was entered into a lottery.
Each lottery drew five winners who each won $20 each.
There were separate lotteries for each question.
The forecasters above the 80 th percentile in accuracy forecasts for each question also received an additional four lottery entries for that question.

The forecasters in the 60 th to 80 th percentile received three additional entries, the forecasters in the 40 th through 60 th percentile received two additional entries, and the forecasters in the 20 th through 40 th percentile received one additional entry.
The Forecasts were scored using mean absolute error, MAE.
Where f represents a forecast and o the outcome:
Results.

In addition to testing the procedure, the primary statistical goal of Pilot Study 1A was to estimate how many total participants we would need to recruit to get a large number of pairwise observations for each pair of questions.
To accomplish this, we focused on the number of questions participants answered in the pilot study, M = 8.54, SD = 12.58.
We modeled these counts by fitting a negative binomial model on the count of how many problems participants to estimate parameters for an expectation (µ = 8.54) and dispersion (θ = 0.47).
We used these parameter estimates to conduct a simulation study.
In each iteration of the simulation we began by simulating participants one at a time.
Each simulated participant was represented by a random draw from the negative binomial distribution defined by the parameters estimated from Pilot 1A: µ = 8.54, θ = 0.47.
This produced a count outcome, which represents the number of questions that simulated participant responded to.

Based on that count, we randomly sampled integers between 1 and 140, representing the question indices that participant would randomly have seen as a participant in the study, and we recorded the question indices that participant responded to, and, more specifically, saved all pairs of questions that participant answered.
The simulation then proceeded to generate another simulated participant and repeat the procedure.

Within each iteration, we repeated this process until the mean number of pairwise observations between pairs of question indices was greater than 100, at which point the iteration terminated and a new iteration began.
The simulation was conducted over 50 iterations.
Results indicated that to achieve a mean of 100 observations for all possible pairs of 140 question indices, the mean number of total participants required would be 8,481, SD = 281.8.
The smallest number of pairwise observations across the 50 iterations had a mean of 66.32, SD = 2.75.

The primary conclusion of this simulation is that if we wished to achieve, on average, 100 pairwise observations between all pairs of 140 questions, we would need to recruit approximately 8,500 participants.
Pilot Study 1B.

Pilot Study 1B repeated the same core design of Pilot Study 1A, but it used all 140 questions instead of just 50, and the goal was to examine the correlational patterns of responses between questions to determine if any potentially loaded onto particular domain knowledge that would favor groups with particular specialized expertise over others if used in the primary study.
Despite collecting additional data, analyses for Pilot Study 1B focused primarily on the accuracy of the forecasts (scored by MAE ), and as a secondary check on the subjective familiarity ratings.
The other variables were collected for potential exploratory analyses and not used in planning subsequent studies, and no analyses involving these variables are reported here.

Based on the results of Pilot Study 1A, we were targeting recruitment of 8,500 participants, but with a primary goal of getting as many pairwise observations between each pair of questions as possible.
Recruitment ran from June 26, 2023 through July 18, 2023, recruiting N = 6,295.
We wound up with a mean of 99.72 observations for each pair of questions, SD = 7.13, with a minimum of 73.
So, although we undershot our target sample size, we functionally achieved our goal of getting an average of 100 observations per pair of questions.
Participants had mean age of 40.67, SD = 14.07, 3,798 (61.5%) female, 2,170 (35.1%) male, 158 gender variant / non-conforming (2.6%), 8 something else (0.1%), 44 (0.8%) prefer not to say.
Procedure.
The procedure was identical to Pilot Study 1A, except with 140 questions instead of 50.
Results.

MAE scores were standardized within question (sMAE ) and winsorized at values of 5 or greater, implying that the forecast was 5 standard deviations less accurate than the mean accuracy for that question, to reduce the influence of outliers on subsequent analyses.
Mean sMAE scores were 0.53, SD = 2.27.
Mean familiarity ratings were 27.11, SD = 27.45.
The correlation between accuracy and familiarity ratings was r = -0.07, suggesting familiarity had a weak correlation with accuracy (lower sMAE scores).

To determine the extent to which specific questions might potentially differentiate specialized expertise, and therefore should be excluded, we conducted exploratory factor analyses (EFAs) on the sMAE scores and familiarity ratings.
We began by conducting a parallel analysis for each set of scores to determine the appropriate number of factors.
In each case, results suggested that three factors were represented at a level greater than chance (see Figure A2 and Figure A3 for scree plots from these analyses).
text.formatted: In each case, results suggested that three factors were represented at a level greater than chance (see Figure <ref type="figure">A2</ref> and Figure <ref type="figure">A3</ref> for scree plots from these analyses).

text.text: In each case, questions with the largest factor loadings had very clear interpretations for one of the first two factors: these questions were highly specialized financial and economic forecasting problems.
We refer to this factor as the economic factor.
The economic factor was the first (largest) factor for the sMAE scores, with 53 questions having factor loadings over 0.40, suggesting accuracy on these questions was highly mutually correlated.

Questions with exceptionally large factor loadings included the closing yield for U.S. Treasuries, the closing value of the Turkish Lira against the U.S. Dollar and the closing stock price of Mercado Libre.
The other two factors didn't have such distinct interpretations, nor as many questions with such high factor loadings for sMAE.
The second factor, which we refer to as a general interest factor, had 18 questions with loadings over 0.40.

Questions with large factor loadings for the second factor included an question about how many migrants will arrive in Europe via the Mediterranean Sea, autonomous vehicle collisions in California, and the number of ACLED recorded protests in Lebanon.

The questions with the largest loadings on the third factor, which we refer to as simply other (10 questions with loadings of at least 0.40) were about OPEC's crude oil production, the number of new privately owned housing units in the U.S., and the U.S.
The pattern was similar for the familiarity ratings, except in this case the economic factor was the second factor rather than the first.
In this case, we refer to the first factor as the general interest factor, and 92 questions had factor loadings of 0.40 or larger.
The questions with the largest loadings were about protests in China, and Influenza cases in Qatar.
The second factor, which was the economic factor, had 49 questions with loadings over 0.40 (32 of which also had loadings over 0.40 for sMAE ).

Questions with the highest loadings included the closing value of the S&P 500, the widest closing spread on 10-year Treasurys below the yield on 2-year Treasurys, and the closing price of Mercado Libre (also one of the largest factor loadings for accuracy).

combined box office gross be.
Table A1 is a correlation matrix between the factor loadings for sMAE and familiarity.

text.text: Worth noting in particular is that the correlations for the same factors (economic and general interest) across the two score types (sMAE and familiarity) are quite large and positive, particularly for the economic factors, and also large and negative between factors both within and between score types.
Discussion.

The key takeaway from the results of Pilot 1B is that, among the 140 questions we initially filtered, a large proportion appear to uniquely filter a specialized type of expertise around finance and economics.
Because the goal is not to develop a financial literacy test, but a generalized test of forecasting proficiency, we want to be careful not to over emphasize these questions.

It remains possible that other questions might also tap into a specialized expertise, but, at least amount the 140 questions we tested, it appears that no topic appears frequently enough and that the questions are evenly distribution enough that no such additional expertise specialization emerges in any such obvious way.
It is also worth noting that there are questions with economic content that did not have large factor loadings on the economic factors.
As such, our primary decision as a result of Pilot Study 1B was to omit the questions that loaded onto the economic factor for either accuracy or familiarity from further consideration.
The economic questions that did eventually wind up in the primary study were not questions that seemed to correlate quite so highly with this particular expertise specialty.

Pilot Study 2 was conducted to aid in planning the design, anticipated attrition rates, and testing of materials ahead of the primary study.
The goal of the primary study was to have approximately 1,000 participants complete all tasks across all seven waves.
To accomplish this, we needed to decide on how many people we needed to recruit at the outset to account for and minimize attrition rates during the primary study.

Thus, the purpose of Pilot Study 2 was to test study design options and incentive schemes to determine which, if any, would minimize attrition, and provide an estimate of how much attrition we might expect during the primary study.
To accomplish this, Pilot Study 2 consisted of three waves: one forecasting wave and two waves of cognitive tasks, each matching content that was also included in the primary study.
Methods.
Participants.
Participants were recruited between September 1, 2023 and September 15, 2023.
We recruited N = 1,199 participants via social media.
Their mean age was 45.06, SD = 13.62, 783 (71.3%) were female, 279 (25.4%) male, 34 (3.1%) gender variant / non conforming, 1 something else, and 1 preferred not to say.
18   Design.
The study followed a 3 (incentive condition) x 2 (recruitment condition) design.
The three incentive conditions were: U-shaped, escalating, and backloaded.
In the U-shaped condition, participants were paid $12.50 for completing the first wave, $5 for completing the second, and $12.50 for completing the third.
In the escalating condition, participants were paid $5 for completing the first wave, $10 for completing the second, and $15 for completing the third.
And in the backloaded condition, participants were paid $5 for completing each of the first two waves, and $20 for completing the third.
In all three conditions, participants received guaranteed payment of $30 (the sum of each individual wave) for completing the full study.

Participants who began with Wave 0 were recruited between September 1 st and 7 th of 2023, and completed two forecasting questions in each of the QEF and PEF.
If they completed Wave 0, they were invited to complete Wave 1 the following week.
Participants not in the Wave 0 condition were recruited between Procedure.
For all participants, Wave 1 was made up of 15 forecasting questions in the QEF.
Questions were drawn from the same item bank as the main study.
See Supplementary list of items for items that were included in Pilot Study 2.
All items had a resolution date at the end of September, 2023.
The 10 participants who made the most accurate forecasts on average were each awarded a $25 bonus.
Waves 2 and 3 were identical to waves 3 and 5 of the primary study.
The 10 participants with the best mean Z -score standardized scores across cognitive tasks within each wave were awarded $25 bonuses.
Results.
Across all conditions, N = 156 completed all three waves.
Figure A4 shows the number of total completions by wave and experimental condition.

text.text: Two key results emerged from Pilot Study 2.
First, attrition was largest between participants' first and second wave and leveled off quickly after that.
This included participants who participated in Wave 0.
By Wave 3, the attrition levels were quite low in the Wave 0 condition, and considerably lower than the condition that did not feature Wave 0.

The results also suggested that the escalating payment condition suffered from lower attrition than the other incentive conditions, particularly compared to the U-shaped condition and in the condition that featured Wave 0.

The escalating payment structure also provides an advantage over the U-shaped condition in terms of expected study cost, as the participants who do attrit out won't ever reach the higher payment waves.

In planning the primary study, this led us to attempt to work backwards and decide how many total participants we would need to recruit to wind up with at least 1,000 people completing all seven waves.

Based on the results from Pilot Study 2, in escalating payment and Wave 0 condition, attrition was just below 30% between Wave 0 and 1, below 20% between Wave 1 and 2, and below 5% between wave 2 and 3.

Because Wave 0 was uncompensated, we worked backwards assuming 5% attrition for all waves after Wave 2, and 20% between waves 1 and 2, and determined that to end with at least 1,000 completers, we needed to target approximately N = 1,660 valid completions from Wave 1 that we would also invite to Wave 2.
