After each choice, there is a certain probability (volatility rate) that whichever option was worth fewer points will increase by 20, "leapfrogging" the previously higher-valued option.
The goal is to select the option worth more points as frequently as possible by deciding how often to sample the unknown option (exploration) versus remain with the known option (exploitation).
the option values are fixed for all participants based on a previously chosen random set of outcomes with a volatility rate of 12.5%.
The AIG version is randomly generated for each participant independently with an equivalent volatility rate and number of trials.

In the computational cognitive psychology literature, LF is typically used to compare individual participants' choice patterns to different model-based decision algorithms, to determine which models best approximate human behavior.

It may be possible to use these model-based approaches to generate scoring rules; however, for simplicity, we scored participants based on the proportion of trials in which they selected the higher option.

The intuition behind the inclusion of LF is that knowing how and when to explore new sources of information rather than exploit familiar ones is a skill that could plausibly benefit forecasting proficiency.
The IQC (Bennett and Steyvers 2022; see also Bereby-Meyer et al. 2003) is made up of a series of general knowledge questions with two possible answers.
text.formatted: The IQC (Bennett and Steyvers 2022; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bereby-Meyer et al. 2003)</ref> is made up of a series of general knowledge questions with two possible answers.

text.text: For most questions, only one of the two answers is factually correct.
For the remaining questions, there is no factually correct answer (impossible questions).
For each question, participants can choose to opt out or answer the question.
If they do answer the question, a confidence rating is also elicited.

The test provides scores for the number of correct answers to the general knowledge questions (GK), judgmental calibration for the confidence judgments (C), and the number of times they chose to opt out of impossible questions (IQ).
The original IQC item bank consists of 100 questions, including six impossible questions.
We generated a shortened anchor version of the IQC using 24 of the questions with correct answers, as well as the six impossible questions.
We then created two additional AIG versions by splitting 48 of the remaining questions from the original item bank in half and supplementing each half with six newly generated impossible questions.
Impossible questions were generated by ChatGPT.
See Appendix D for a list of the newly generated questions and the prompt used to generate them.
The intuition behind the inclusion of the IQC is that knowing the extent of one's knowledge and having well-calibrated confidence are skills that could plausibly benefit forecasting proficiency.
Denominator Neglect (DN).
DN was inspired by a common decision bias of the same name.
Participants make a series of choices between two proportions with the goal of selecting the larger proportion.
Research indicates that people will tend to erroneously favor proportions that have larger numerators, even when they represent smaller proportions (Stanovich and West 2008).
text.formatted: Research indicates that people will tend to erroneously favor proportions that have larger numerators, even when they represent smaller proportions <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Stanovich and West 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Inclusion of visual arrays can reduce denominator neglect (Garcia-Retamero et al. 2010).
text.formatted: Inclusion of visual arrays can reduce denominator neglect <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Garcia-Retamero et al. 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Each DN item features a choice between two boxes with a mix of gold and silver coins.
The goal is to select the box with a larger proportion of gold coins.
One box always contains 10 total coins (the small denominator option) with either one, two, or three gold coins.

The other box always has 400 total coins (the large denominator option), with proportions ranging from plus (harmony trials) or minus (conflict trials) 1% to 8% the small denominator option in intervals of 1%.
There are two different designs of DN: separate (S) and combined (C).
In the separate design, options have only a verbal description or a visual array, but not both.
Items can either be heterogeneous (one option verbal and the other visual) or homogeneous (both options verbal or both options visual).
In the combined design, each option is represented by both a verbal description and a visual array.
Both designs have an anchor and an AIG version.
The anchor version of the separate design consists of a single set of randomly generated items.
The AIG version randomizes whether and how each item will be homogeneous or heterogeneous independently for each participant.

The anchor version of the combined design consists of a fixed set of randomly generated small denominator option proportions (10%, 20%, and 30%), and the AIG version randomly generates these proportions independently for each participant.
Each design of DN has 48 items.
DN is scored as the total number of cases in which the larger proportion is selected.
Success on DN is driven by how well one understands the importance of total population sizes, or base rates, when judging event outcomes.

The intuition behind the inclusion of DN is that being aware of the importance of base rates and their implications for making probabilistic decisions is a skill that could plausibly benefit forecasting proficiency.
BU is based on experiments by Phillips and Edwards (1966) in which participants must iteratively update their probabilistic judgments based on new information.
text.formatted: BU is based on experiments by <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Phillips and Edwards (1966)</ref> in which participants must iteratively update their probabilistic judgments based on new information.

text.text: Two boxes are displayed: one containing p red balls and 100 -p blue balls, the other containing p blue balls and 100 -p red balls, with p randomly set to either 60 or 70.
At the start of each trial, one of the boxes is chosen at random with equal probability, but it is not revealed to participants which box it is.
Five balls are then drawn from the chosen box, one at a time, with replacement.
After the fifth draw, the task resets, and a new trial begins.
The test has two designs, easy and hard, each of which consists of eight trials with five sequential decisions.
In the easy design, after each ball is drawn, participants report the probability that the chosen box is the majority blue box.
In the hard design, participants report the probability that the next draw will be a blue ball.
Each design also has an AIG and an anchor version.
In the anchor version, the sequence of draws is fixed for all participants, while in the AIG version, the draws are randomly generated for each participant independently.
BU scores are based on the absolute deviation between the estimate made in each trial and the optimal Bayesian estimate (see Appendix G for scoring details).

The intuition behind the inclusion of BU is that following normative rules about how and how much to update one's probabilistic beliefs is a skill that could plausibly benefit forecasting proficiency.
Competence (ADMC) inventory is a battery of tests designed to assess decision-making ability (Bruine de Bruin et al. 2007).
text.formatted: Competence (ADMC) inventory is a battery of tests designed to assess decision-making ability (Bruine de <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bruin et al. 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Though the ADMC is well validated, to our knowledge it has not previously been included in any forecasting studies.
RF is one of three subscales we considered for the FPT.
The RF subscale consists of a series of comparisons between two options.
Each comparison is repeated at two different points during the ADMC: once in a positive frame and again in a negative frame.

For each comparison, participants rate their preference for the options on a scale of 1 to 6, with 1 representing extreme preference for the first option and 6 extreme preference for the second option.
Scores are based on consistency in judgment across the positively and negatively framed versions of each comparison.
The ADMC-RF was adapted exactly as described in Bruine de Bruin et al. (2007), with the positively and negatively framed versions of each comparison split between the two cognitive test blocks.
text.formatted: The ADMC-RF was adapted exactly as described in Bruine de <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bruin et al. (2007)</ref>, with the positively and negatively framed versions of each comparison split between the two cognitive test blocks.

text.text: The intuition behind the inclusion of ADMC-RF is that resisting the effects of irrelevant information, such as how information is framed, is a skill that could plausibly benefit forecasting proficiency.
The RC subscale of the ADMC is similar to one of the CFS testlets: it assesses the consistency of risk assessments across timeframes.
Participants are asked to assess the probability that several events occur within a series of increasing time horizons.
For each event, they first rate the probability that it will occur within one year.
Later in the test, the same events are repeated, except participants must report the probability that they will occur within three years.
The same events are later repeated once more with a time horizon of five years.
Judgments are considered consistent when the probabilities monotonically increase for longer time horizons.
The ADMC-RC was adapted exactly as described in Bruine de Bruin et al. (2007).
text.formatted: The ADMC-RC was adapted exactly as described in Bruine de <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bruin et al. (2007)</ref>.

text.text: The intuition behind the inclusion of ADMC-RC is that following the normative rules of probability judgment is a skill that is known to benefit forecasting accuracy, and this test operationalizes that in a slightly different way than the CFS.
In the DR subscale of the ADMC, participants must assess how consumers should make purchasing decisions based on a set of stated preferences.
Each consumer specifies how they prioritize a set of feature ratings for a product they wish to purchase.
Participants must then decide which of several options best satisfies the consumer's preferences.
The ADMC-DR was adapted exactly as described in Bruine de Bruin et al. (2007), with one small modification: the product targets were televisions rather than DVD players.
text.formatted: The ADMC-DR was adapted exactly as described in Bruine de <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bruin et al. (2007)</ref>, with one small modification: the product targets were televisions rather than DVD players.

text.text: The intuition behind the inclusion of the ADMC-DR is that being able to optimize judgments based on an set of explicitly stated rules is a skill that could plausibly benefit forecasting proficiency.
GL is designed to assess how well subjects make inferences from visual representations of data (Galesic and Garcia-Retamero 2011).
text.formatted: GL is designed to assess how well subjects make inferences from visual representations of data <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Galesic and Garcia-Retamero 2011)</ref>.

text.text: It was originally developed in the context of medical decision-making and to our knowledge has not been previously validated in the context of a forecasting study.
The test was adapted exactly as described in Galesic and Garcia-Retamero (2011).

Denominator neglect is a known decision bias in which people rate proportions that are smaller as being superior if they have larger absolute values in the numerator (Stanovich and West 2008).
text.formatted: Denominator neglect is a known decision bias in which people rate proportions that are smaller as being superior if they have larger absolute values in the numerator <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Stanovich and West 2008)</ref>.

text.text: For example, a 9 in 100 chance to win a lottery will be rated as superior to a chance of 1 in 10.
Additional research has shown that visual arrays in addition to verbal representations reduce denominator neglect (Garcia-Retamero et al. 2010).

text.text: Our version of the task is framed as a choice between two boxes with a mixture of gold and silver coins.
Selecting a gold coin is considered a success, and a silver coin a failure.

There are two versions of the task: one in which each option is either represented by only a verbal description or a visual representation (with each option randomized in each trial), and one where each option is represented by both a verbal description and visual representation.
In each case, the small denominator lottery is based on a denominator of 10, with the proportion of successes being 10%, 20%, or 30%.

The large denominator lottery is based on a denominator of 400, with the proportions ranging from plus or minus 1% to 8% of the small lottery (in intervals of 1%), for a total of 48 trials per version.
The primary Denominator Neglect Score (DN) is the total number of cases in which the larger proportion is selected.

Time Series.

This task is based on work by De Baets and Vanderheyden (2021) and Reimers and Harvey (2011) in which people are asked to extrapolate from graphical time series using a visual point-and-click interface.

text.text: On each trial, participants will see historical data from an unnamed time series, generated by an underlying function with added noise, and be required to predict the subsequent five points in the trend.

The task is a 2 (noise level: high vs low) x 2 (direction: ascending or descending) x 2 (type: linear or exponential) x 2 (historical data: 10 points or 30 points) design, with one item for each combination per form, and two forms (a 16 item anchor form and a 16 item AIG form).
Primary Time Series Scores (TS) are computed as the Mean Squared Deviation from the generative function.
Other potential scoring options include proneness to known biases such as trend damping and adding noise, which may be included in exploratory analyses.
Exploratory analyses will also compare the effectiveness of scores from different conditions in terms of how well they predict accuracy.
Leapfrog.
The leapfrog task is a tractable bandit-style task designed to measure optimal explore vs exploit tendencies (Knox et al. 2012).
text.formatted: The leapfrog task is a tractable bandit-style task designed to measure optimal explore vs exploit tendencies <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Knox et al. 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The task is a set of binary choices between two options.
To start, one option is worth 0 points and the other is worth 10 points.
Each time a choice is selected, its point value is revealed, but the alternative not chosen remains hidden.
After each choice, there is a certain probability (volatility rate) whichever option was worth fewer points will "leapfrog" the option worth more points and increase by 20.
So if option A is originally 10 and option B 0, at some point option B will become 20 while A remains 10.
Then A will eventually become 30 while B stays at 20.
The goal is to select the option worth more points as frequently as possible.
The Anchor form will consist of 200 trials in which the option values are pre-determined based on a random set of outcomes with a volatility rate of 12.5%.
The AIG form will be a randomly generated series with an equivalent volatility rate and number of trials.
Primary Leapfrog Scores (LF) are based on the proportion of trials in which participants selected the higher option.
There are also several model based assessments of optimal decision making which can be explored (see Knox et al. 2012).

The other contains p blue balls and 100 -p red balls (in our version, p is either 60 or 70).
One of the boxes is chosen at random with equal probability.
Five balls are drawn one at a time with replacement.
The task has two versions.
In the Source version, after each drawn ball, subjects must report the probability that the box is the majority red or majority blue box.
In the Forecast version, subjects must report the probability the next draw will be a blue ball.
